Onboarding — round 3

One design, argued. The stance: onboarding asks for one decision per screen, and nothing ever moves. New layouts and compositions throughout; the Cairo Nights language, the token set and the HeroUI Native catalogue are unchanged — every control below maps to an installed primitive or an existing src/components/ui wrapper.

MA-onboarding-redesign · pre-gate-1 · 390 pt frames · fonts substituted (Sora → Avenir Next, Inter → Helvetica Neue) because the published artifact blocks external hosts. Rationale, costs, and the decisions I need from you are at the bottom of this page.

A · The shell

Four tracks with fixed dimensions on all four routes: header 56, progress rail 55, a flexible content viewport, and a footer of 2-line status track + 52 pt CTA. The status track is the load-bearing idea and the reason this redesign does not pay for stability in dead space: it is always mounted and never empty. Idle it carries the one footnote that screen genuinely wants; on failure the error replaces that footnote inside the identical box. No reservation cost, no reflow when something breaks.

The footnote is real content, not a placeholder held open for an error that may never arrive. That is why the reservation is free: A3 occupies the same box without pushing the CTA a single pixel.
Per-screen idle copy — N1 “You can change this later in Settings.” · N2 “Saved on this phone. Nothing is uploaded.” · N3 “One account is enough to start.” · N4 “This is your starting point, not your net worth.”

Idle. Tapping the CTA advances the step. The line differs per screen and always says something usable.

A3 · Status track, failed error
⚠Couldn't save that. Your account is safe — tap Review setup to try again.
Review setup
Retry is the CTA itself, so no second button ever appears and the footer never grows. Two lines of danger-coloured copy is the widest case the track must hold — measured against the longest error string, not guessed.
Contrast: --danger #E05A42 on --background = 4.81:1 — passes AA for body text. The track is announced as a live region so a screen reader hears the failure without moving focus.

Failure. Same box, same height, same CTA position. Tapping the CTA retries the failed step — it never re-inserts an account.

B · N1 — Welcome

Not a splash — a decision screen, so it looks like one: the mark, one claim, two option rows. The illustration is gone; it cost a third of the viewport and moved nobody forward. Currency is a RadioGroup of two card rows, not Tabs — a tablist announces "the content below switches", which is false here, and radio semantics give the selected state for free. Each row states the consequence of the choice in its own words rather than making the user infer it.

B4 · Empty n/a — by rule
N1 has no empty state.
Business rule 5 pre-selects EGP, so the screen is fully populated on first paint and there is nothing to load. App startup owns migrations, the onboarding store and the account snapshot before any onboarding route mounts, so N1 never renders a skeleton either.
Drawing an invented blank frame here would misrepresent the flow. The only states this screen has beyond the default are B2 and B3.
If startup itself fails, the existing app-level startup error screen owns it — outside this scope.

Stated, not drawn — deliberately. The four-state floor exists to catch forgotten states, not to license invented ones.

C · N2 — Add your first account shared form

This is where first-run onboarding is actually abandoned, so this is where the design spends. Three moves. One: account type is a plain 3-column grid, 5 tiles, left-aligned — not a centred matrix. Full labels at 12 px, 114 × 76 pt targets, one layout at every text size (the old design needed a separate two-column fallback for accessibility sizes; this one grows in place instead). Two: every field owns a permanent 20 pt message rail. Helper copy lives there when the field is clean and the error takes the same rail when it isn't, so an error swaps text rather than inserting a row. Three: the credit-card block has a reserved slot in a fixed position — a dashed one-line hint when the type isn't Credit Card, the real fields in the same place when it is. The user learns the card path is heavier before committing to it, and the fields appear where the hint was rather than the page silently growing below the fold.

APR appears inside the card block, below the switch — the block grows downward and the header, rail and CTA are untouched. Two failures at once: a field-level error in its own rail, and a save-level error in the status track. They never fight for the same space.

What I deliberately dropped: the July field list had both “Amount currently owed” and a separate “revolving balance”. Two “how much do you owe” boxes on someone's first-ever screen is a comprehension trap, and I have never seen a first-run user fill the second one correctly. Balance relabels to Amount currently owed and that is the only owed field. If the revolving_balance column must be non-null at creation, [layla] decides what it derives from — it should not become a fifth question.

D · The 32-colour sheet

The July design put the 32 swatches in two horizontally scrolling rows. I'm rejecting that: a picker that hides half its options behind a scroll gets the first visible option picked, every time. Instead — all 32 visible at once, no scrolling, as an 8-column chart of rounded tiles. Column position means the same family in both blocks, so Nile Teal rich sits directly above Nile Teal soft. Tiles, not dots: a tile fills its cell, which makes the colours comparable and the targets bigger for free. The cost is that the picker looks like a paint chart rather than like the dots it produces — a trade I'll take, because choosing a colour and reading a colour are different jobs.

The tick is near-black on Sand soft and bone-white on Nile rich in D1 — picked per swatch from a contrast table, never assumed white. The selection ring is drawn in the cell's permanent 3 pt padding, so selecting never resizes a tile or reflows the grid.

Geometry and targets. 8 columns at 390 pt with 16 pt sheet padding and a 4 pt gap gives a cell of 41.25 × 44. That is 2.75 pt short of the 44 pt floor on the horizontal axis, so each cell carries hitSlop={{left: 2, right: 2}} → 45.25 × 44 effective, with no overlap because the gap is 4. Colour is never the only signal: the preview row names the family and tone, and each tile's accessibility label reads “Nile Teal, rich, selected”. Sheet uses the project Sheet at size="md" with a sticky footer; the grid does not scroll, so there is no gorhom scrollable inside it at all.

E · N3 — Add more accounts

The July version led with a celebration illustration. This one leads with the list, because the only question on this screen is “is anything missing?” and you answer that by looking at what you've entered. Success is one 28 pt chip, not a hero. Each row shows the account's balance in its own currency — no running total here, because a total needs a rate and a rate might not exist. Deferring that to N4 keeps this screen honest and keeps the conversion problem in exactly one place.

F · N4 — Ready to start

The value-slot problem. One slot has to hold EGP 148,250.00, −EGP 1,234,567.89, and the sentence Exchange rate needed. Size the slot to a number and the sentence reflows; size it to the sentence and the number looks apologetic. My answer is a two-slot stack with fixed heights: a 40 pt value slot and a 34 pt caption slot, and three rules that keep both honest.

One — the value slot never wraps. One line, vertically centred, 31 px Sora. Long amounts step down to 22 px rather than wrapping (F4). Exchange rate needed renders at that same 22 px step with a warning glyph, so it lands inside a box already proven to hold a 22 px line. Two — the caption slot is never empty. Reserving two lines for a caption that only appears in one state would be dead space in the other six, so every state has a caption that earns it: what converted, why it's negative, why it's zero. The reservation costs nothing because it is always doing work. Three — the number is never coloured. Not red for negative, not green for positive. This is a position, not a change, and the first number MoneyApp ever shows a person who legitimately owns a credit card should not be painted as a failure. The sign carries the fact; the caption carries the meaning. What that costs: no colour-coded scanning — irrelevant for one number you read once, and something to revisit if this hero is ever reused on the dashboard.

The summary is preserved through the failure — the hero does not blank, skeleton, or recompute. Retry is the same CTA and re-runs only the completion write.

N4 has no empty state and no content loading state. Zero accounts on N4 resolves to N2 before the route paints (same guard as E3), and the summary is computed from a snapshot startup already loaded, so there is nothing to wait for. F8 is a transition loading state, not a content one. If [layla]'s computation ever becomes async, the value slot gets a Skeleton at exactly 40 pt and the caption slot one at 34 pt — the slots are already the right shape for it.

Rationale

The stance, and what it costs

First-run onboarding is abandoned at the form, not at the welcome. People tolerate one screen of pitch; they do not tolerate a form whose length they cannot see the end of, or one that moves under their thumb. So the design spends its budget on N2 and N4 and starves N1 and N3 deliberately.

What that costs. N1 lost its illustration, so the app's first screen is more sober than the July version — it is a decision screen, not a welcome mat. If you want warmth on first launch, this is where it went, and I'd argue the warmth belongs in the copy and the mark rather than in 250 pt of vector art the user scrolls past. N3 lost its celebration hero and kept a 28 pt chip. And the credit-card hint row (C1) costs ~60 pt of permanent vertical space on the four account types that will never use it, to buy the one thing that matters: the card fields appear where the placeholder was, and the user knows before choosing that Credit Card is the longer road. The cheaper version: delete the hint row, let the block appear from nothing. It saves 60 pt and reintroduces exactly the surprise-growth defect this scope exists to fix. I don't recommend it, but it is a real option and it is free.

Every control maps to something that already exists

Ran npm run ui:inventory before drawing anything. Nothing below is custom, and nothing needs a new dependency.

ElementPrimitive / wrapper
Route shellproject Screen / ScreenScroll
Headerproject StackHeader (N1 swaps the back button for the mark, same track)
Progress railmodule-local View — HeroUI has no stepper; standing exception
Currency choiceRadioGroup + RadioGroup.Item + Radio + Label + Description
Account type gridRadioGroup, item render-prop for isSelected; grid via style
Text / amount fieldsproject Input → HeroUI TextField · Input · Label · Description · FieldError
Currency fieldHeroUI Select
Colour trigger rowListGroup.Item + ItemPrefix / ItemContent / ItemSuffix
ElementPrimitive / wrapper
Colour sheetproject Sheet (size="md", sticky footer) → HeroUI BottomSheet
Colour tilesPressableFeedback in a styled grid
Card details blockSurface + Separator; Chip for the field count
Interest trackingHeroUI Switch — the grey RN Switch is deleted
Account & summary rowsListGroup + Separator
N4 heroproject HeroShell — gradient, 26 px grid and corner glow all already exist
All CTAsproject Button (+ Spinner while busy)
N3 empty guardproject EmptyState

Two notes. The July decision to use Tabs for currency is reversed — RadioGroup is the correct semantic and gives 76 pt targets with a description line per option; Tabs would announce a tablist for something that isn't one. And the status track is plain Typography, not Alert: Alert is a bordered box with its own padding, so putting it in the footer would make the footer taller in the error state — the exact defect the track exists to prevent. The existing ColorSwatchPicker becomes the sheet's grid or is deleted; the three divergent swatch-row implementations named in scope.md collapse to one. The N4 “decorative gradient circle” is not a new element — it is HeroShell's existing corner glow, free.

Where I reached outside the token set

Five places, all named rather than quietly absorbed.

1 · The token script doesn't emit everything. Colors.shared (the hero gradient stops) and AcctTokens (the account palette) are real tokens in theme.ts / theme_tokens.ts but design:tokens omits both. I re-declared them in a clearly-labelled second :root block with each source file named. Worth teaching the script to emit them.
2 · Four of the sixteen colour families don't exist yet. AcctTokens ships 12. Jade, Indigo, Coral and Graphite come from the July functional doc and need adding — no migration, colours are stored as plain hex values.
3 · There is no input-height token. HeroUI's Input derives its height from padding and font size, so “44” is not written down anywhere. I drew fields at Size.dialogButton (44), which happens to equal TouchSize.min. It renders correctly but it's a semantic borrow; an alias Size.fieldHeight = ms(44) would say what it means.
4 · The three geometry numbers that make the zero-shift contract testable are not tokens. The field message rail (20), the N4 value slot (40) and the N4 caption slot (34). These are the load-bearing values in this entire design and they should be Size.fieldMessageTrack, Size.summaryValueSlot and Size.summaryCaptionSlot so a unit test can assert them rather than device QA having to eyeball them. This is my one real ask. Three constants.
5 · Fonts. The published artifact blocks external hosts, so this page renders Avenir Next for Sora and Helvetica Neue for Inter. Both are geometrically close but Sora is wider and squarer at display sizes — the N4 hero number and the N1 headline will look slightly different on device, which is a gate-3 check, not a gate-1 one. Composed sizes like the option-row and tile min-heights are token arithmetic (Size.dialogButton + Spacing.xxl), which is legal, not a new value.

Accessibility — including one finding you should decide on

Contrast, computed not assumed. Against --background #0F1923: --foreground ≈ 18:1 · --warning 9.09:1 · --accent 7.78:1 · --success 6.56:1 · --danger 4.81:1. All pass AA. --muted is 2.36:1 — decorative only; it is the progress-rail track and never carries text.

The finding: --content-secondary #6B7F99 computes 4.33:1 on --background and 3.77:1 on --surface. Both are below the 4.5:1 AA floor for text under 18.66 px. It clears AA-large (3:1) and misses AA-normal by about 4%. Inside onboarding I've handled it by rule: anything a user must read is --foreground, and --content-secondary is confined to genuinely redundant labels — the rail line that repeats the header title, “optional” tags, the account-type line under a row that also carries a colour dot and an amount. Hierarchy is carried by size and weight instead of colour, which is why the screens read as flatter than the July version. Lightening the token would fix it everywhere in one line, but it touches every screen in the app, so it is yours to call, not mine.

Targets. Currency rows 358 × 76 · type tiles 114 × 76 · all fields and the colour trigger 44 tall · colour tiles 41.25 × 44 with hitSlop 2 horizontally → 45.25 × 44 · back button 36 visual with hitSlop 8 → 52 (existing StackHeader). The one to verify in review is HeroUI's BottomSheet.Close — it renders a size="sm" icon button and may need hitSlop to clear 44.

Dynamic type. Fixed tracks (header, rail, CTA) use explicit line-height and numberOfLines. Everything else grows into the scroll viewport and is never clipped: type-tile labels take a second line and the grid row grows in place — no separate two-column accessibility layout, which the July design needed and this one doesn't. The field message rail is a minimum height, not a fixed one, so long error copy at large text sizes expands rather than truncating. Progress announces “Step 2 of 4”; the segments themselves are hidden from assistive tech. Swatches announce “Nile Teal, rich, selected”. The status track is a live region. Entrance motion is opacity only, and none at all under reduce-motion.

What I am deliberately not building

The separate revolving balance field (folded into “Amount currently owed”). An inline “add a rate” action on N4 — it would pull a currency screen into onboarding to fix a state the dashboard already handles. A two-page credit form, which would eliminate conditional expansion entirely and is the most robust answer to the geometry problem — rejected because it adds a mode to the shared form that Settings would inherit, for a path only some users take. Horizontally scrolling swatch rows. The N1 illustration. Any entrance animation that translates or scales. And no running total on N3, because a total needs a rate.

What I need you to decide

1 · What USD actually promises — scope.md open question 2, and it is a copy decision with branding weight so it is explicitly yours. I've designed for the cheap answer: the screen asks “Which currency do you think in?” and each option states a display consequence (“Every total in the app is shown in EGP” / “Totals convert to USD using the rate you save”). That is honest under the current architecture, where EGP is the storage currency. The expensive answer — base currency meaning the same thing in every module — reaches well outside this scope. Say the word if you want the expensive one and it becomes its own scope.
2 · --content-secondary. Leave it and follow my usage rule inside onboarding, or lighten the token app-wide. Cross-scope either way.
3 · 32 colours or 24? Sixteen families needs four new entries in AcctTokens. Twelve families × two tones = 24 swatches and fits the same 8-column grid in 3 rows with no new tokens at all. Cheaper; I prefer 32, because at 24 the picker no longer reads as a complete chart.
4 · The logo accent. I've drawn the Cross Fan mark with the teal dot moved onto the card corner rather than over the stem of the folded M (open question 1) — it stops reading as “Mi” at launcher size. Confirm or revert.
5 · The credit-card hint row. 60 pt permanently, on four types out of five. Keep or cut.
